why_how.text: Parallel parking appears on every New York road test, so every applicant must be able to do it.
Backup cameras and sensors only assist; the driver stays responsible and checks behind before every reverse.

scenario.text: Ana finds a space on her side of the street and wants to back into it behind a parked car.

reasoning.text: She checks her mirrors, signals, stops about two feet beside the lead car, checks both shoulders, then creeps back at full curb lock.

result.text: When her front wheels are opposite the lead bumper she counter-steers, stops short of the rear car, and centers within a foot of the curb.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a backup camera means you no longer have to check behind yourself.

correction.text: The aids assist, but the driver stays ultimately responsible and must check behind before every reverse.

memory_support.text: Two feet beside, full lock back, one foot from the curb.

prompt.text: You are parallel parking and your front wheels are now opposite the lead car's rear bumper. What do you do next?

answer.text: Counter-steer while backing, clear the lead car, stop short of the rear car, then straighten and center.

rationale.text: That step ends with the wheels at most one foot from the curb.

lines.text: A skill on every road test.

narration.text: Welcome to the parallel parking lesson. The manual says parallel parking appears on every New York road test, so this is a skill every applicant has to show. The same test also expects you to know where parking is illegal and what the three no-series signs mean, and those come in later lessons. Here we focus on the parking itself: choosing a space, setting up beside the car ahead, backing in at full lock, counter-steering into the space, centering close to the curb, and the small adjustments that follow. We start with a word about the cameras and sensors many cars now carry.

Many cars now have backup cameras, parking sensors, or even self-parking aids. The manual is clear about where they fit. These aids assist with backing, but the driver stays ultimately responsible for what happens. That means you must still check behind you before every reverse, every single time, no matter what the screen or the beeping tells you. The aids help you see more, but the duty to look before reversing stays with you. With that settled, let's set up for the back-in itself, starting with how to choose a space that fits your car on your side of the road.

lines.text: Pick a fitting space on your side.
Stop about two feet beside the lead car.

narration.text: Start by picking a space on your side of the street that is big enough for your car. Check your mirrors and signal so drivers behind you know what you plan. Then pull up and stop about two feet beside the lead vehicle, the car parked in front of the space. Before you move back, check over both shoulders for people and traffic. Now creep backward slowly with the wheel turned fully toward the curb, watching through the rear window and glancing to the side and front as you go. Keep watching through the rear window the whole time, with quick side and front glances, as the car eases back toward the space.

lines.text: Front wheels opposite the lead bumper.

narration.text: The next moment comes when your front wheels are opposite the lead car's rear bumper. Now you counter-steer, turning the wheel the other way while you keep backing, so the front of your car swings in behind the lead car and clears it. Stop before you reach the car parked behind you. Then straighten the wheels and pull forward or back a little to center yourself in the space. The manual sets a clear target for the finish: your wheels should end up no more than one foot from the curb. That one-foot gap is the number to remember for this step.

lines.text: About two feet beside the lead car.
At most one foot from the curb.

narration.text: Here is a trap worth noticing. Two different gaps appear in this procedure, and they are easy to mix up. The first is the setup gap: you stop about two feet beside the lead vehicle before you start backing. The second is the finish: once you have counter-steered and centered, your wheels should be at most one foot from the curb. If you are still too far out, the manual says to adjust by alternating forward and reverse, steering toward the curb and then straight. And while you sit there, keep the road-side doors shut against cyclists and passing traffic.

lines.text: Front wheels opposite the lead bumper.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are backing into a parallel space and your front wheels are now opposite the rear bumper of the lead car. What do you do next? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to counter-steer while you keep backing. That swings the front of your car in so you clear the lead car. Then you stop short of the car behind you, straighten the wheels, and center yourself in the space with your wheels no more than one foot from the curb. The setup gap of about two feet beside the lead car is a different number, so keep the two apart.

lines.text: Aids help; you still check behind.
Two feet beside, one foot from curb.

narration.text: Let's pull this lesson together. Parallel parking is on every New York road test. Cameras and sensors may help, but you stay responsible and check behind before every reverse. Set up about two feet beside the lead car, check both shoulders, and back in at full lock. When your front wheels reach the lead bumper, counter-steer, clear the lead car, stop short of the rear car, then straighten and center with your wheels at most one foot from the curb. Adjust nearer by rocking forward and back, and keep road-side doors shut against cyclists and traffic. Next we park on a hill and leave.

why_how.text: Hill parking angles the wheels to the curb so a rolling car is blocked from moving into traffic.
Leaving a space uses its own scan order, right shoulder first and left shoulder last.

scenario.text: Luis is parked between two cars and wants to pull out into traffic.

reasoning.text: He straightens his wheels, backs toward the rear car, swings his wheels away from the curb, then scans right shoulder, interior mirror, signal, side mirror and left shoulder.

result.text: He rolls out slowly past the front car and merges after a last left-shoulder check.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the usual left-first glance when pulling out of a parallel space.

correction.text: Space exits scan the right shoulder first and the left shoulder last, reversing the habit of an ordinary lane change.

memory_support.text: On a hill, wheels to the curb; leaving, right first, left last.

prompt.text: You are about to pull out of a parallel space. Which shoulder do you check first?

answer.text: The right shoulder, through the rear window.

rationale.text: Exits start with the right shoulder and end with the left, the reverse of a lane change.

lines.text: Securing a car on a hill.

narration.text: This lesson covers two moments that bookend any parking job. First, what to do when the space you chose is on a hill, so the car stays put while you are away. Second, how to leave a parallel space and rejoin traffic safely. The manual gives a short checklist for the hill and a careful order of glances and signals for the exit. That exit order has a twist: it does not follow the usual habit you use for an ordinary lane change. We will start with the hill, then set up the exit, then walk the scan order, and finally look at why the order runs the other way.

lines.text: Angle the wheels to the curb.

narration.text: When you park on a hill, the manual gives three steps. Set the brake. Select Park, or first gear if you drive a manual. Then angle your wheels to the curb. The reason is stated right in the rule: angled wheels block any roll toward traffic. So the brake, the gear and the wheel angle all go together each time you park on a slope, and the wheel angle is what keeps a roll from heading into traffic. Brake, gear and wheels to the curb is the whole hill checklist. With the car secured, let's turn to the other end of the job, getting ready to pull out of a parallel space and rejoin the lane.

lines.text: Swing wheels away from the curb.

narration.text: Before you merge out of a parallel space, prepare the car. Straighten the wheels first. Then back up toward the vehicle behind you. Now swing your wheels away from the curb so the car is pointed out toward the lane. Notice the contrast with the hill: when parking on a hill the wheels angle to the curb, while leaving a space they swing away from it. So the exit setup is straighten, back toward the rear vehicle, then swing out. Only after this setup do you start the scans and signals that tell you when it is safe to move out, and that sequence is our next slide.

lines.text: Right shoulder through the rear window.

narration.text: The manual lays out the order for a safe entry into traffic from a parallel space. Begin with a scan over your right shoulder through the rear window. Watch the interior mirror. Turn on your signal. Scan the side mirror. Then look over your left shoulder as you roll forward slowly, clearing the car in front of you. Finally, with one more left-shoulder check, merge when it is safe. So the order runs right shoulder, interior mirror, signal, side mirror, left shoulder while rolling slowly, and a final left-shoulder check before the merge.

lines.text: Step one: check right shoulder first.
Steps five and six: check left shoulder.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Leaving a parallel space follows a specific six-step scan order. The exit scan starts with your right shoulder and ends with your left. The manual calls this out directly: space exits scan the right shoulder first and the left shoulder last. If you fall back on the left-first habit, you skip the opening right-side check through the rear window. So when you are parked at the curb and ready to go, deliberately start on the right, work through the mirrors and signal, and finish on the left.

lines.text: Ready to leave a parallel space.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are parked at the curb in a parallel space and you are ready to pull out into traffic. Which shoulder do you check first? Work it out before reading on. The answer is your right shoulder, scanning through the rear window. After that comes the interior mirror, the signal, the side mirror, and then the left shoulder as you roll out slowly past the front car and merge. Make sure to begin with the right-shoulder check before mirrors and signal, and finish with the left-shoulder checks.

lines.text: Hill: brake, gear, wheels to curb.

narration.text: Let's wrap up. On a hill, set the brake, select Park or first gear, and angle the wheels to the curb so any roll is blocked from traffic. To leave a parallel space, straighten the wheels, back toward the rear vehicle, and swing the wheels away from the curb. Then follow the exit order: right shoulder through the rear window, interior mirror, signal, side mirror, and the left shoulder as you roll slowly past the front car, with a final left-shoulder check before you merge. Next we look at the no-series signs.

why_how.text: The three no-series signs are part of what the road test expects you to know.
Each term has its own meaning, so each sign allows a different kind of brief stop.

scenario.text: Priya wants to drop off a friend where a no standing sign is posted.

reasoning.text: No standing allows brief people loading with the driver aboard, so she may let her friend out while she stays in the car.

result.text: She stops briefly, her friend gets out, and she drives on without leaving the car.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating no parking, no standing and no stopping as if they meant the same thing.

correction.text: They form a ladder: no parking allows brief loading, no standing allows only brief people loading with the driver aboard, and no stopping allows only required halts.

memory_support.text: Parking, standing, stopping: each step allows less.

prompt.text: Under a no stopping sign, when may you halt?

answer.text: Only for traffic devices, officers, or to avoid a collision.

rationale.text: No stopping is the top of the ladder and bans everything but those required halts.

narration.text: This lesson is about three words that sound alike but mean different things in New York: parking, standing and stopping. The manual ties them to the three no-series signs, which the road test also expects you to know. Once you have the three definitions straight, each sign makes sense, because each one bans a little more than the one before it. We will define each term, then see what each sign still allows, then line them up as a ladder from least strict to most strict. By the end you should be able to read any of these signs and know whether a quick stop is allowed.

lines.text: Parking: brief goods or people stops excepted.
Standing: brief stops for people only.

narration.text: Start with the definitions. Parking means your vehicle is stopped, except when you stop briefly to load or unload goods or people. Standing means you are stopped briefly for people only, picking someone up or letting someone out. Stopping is the broadest word of all: it means any halt, however short. So parking already excludes brief loading, standing narrows the brief stop down to people, and stopping covers every halt you could make. Keep those three in mind, because the signs on the next slide are built directly on them, one sign for each word.

lines.text: No parking: brief goods or people loading.
No standing: brief people loading, driver aboard.

narration.text: Now apply the definitions to the signs. In a no parking zone you may still stop briefly to load or unload goods or people. In a no standing zone you may stop briefly to pick up or drop off people, and the driver stays aboard. In a no stopping zone you may halt only when a traffic device or an officer requires it, or to avoid a collision. So the question to ask at any of these signs is simple: what am I stopping for, and will I stay in the car? The answer tells you whether the sign allows it. Brief goods loading fits only the no parking sign, a brief people stop with the driver aboard fits no standing as well, and only a required halt fits no stopping.

Here is the trap. Because the three signs look alike, people treat them as interchangeable. The manual describes them as a three-step tightening ladder instead. No parking bans everything except brief loading. No standing goes further and also bans goods loading and the driver getting out. No stopping bans everything except the halts you are obeying, for devices, officers or collision avoidance. So a stop that is fine under no parking, like briefly unloading packages, is not allowed under no standing. And a quick passenger drop-off allowed under no standing is not allowed under no stopping.

lines.text: A no stopping sign is posted.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving along a street posted with a no stopping sign. When may you halt there? Work it out before reading on. The answer is only when a traffic device or an officer requires it, or when you must stop to avoid a collision. You may not stop to drop off a passenger or to unload goods, because no stopping sits at the top of the ladder and bans everything except those required halts. A brief passenger drop-off with the driver aboard belongs under no standing, and brief goods loading belongs under no parking.

title.text: Read the sign, know the stop

lines.text: Each sign allows less than the last.

narration.text: To close, parking means stopped except briefly for goods or people, standing means stopped briefly for people only, and stopping means any halt at all. The signs follow those words. No parking still allows brief loading of goods or people. No standing allows only brief people loading with the driver aboard. No stopping allows only halts for traffic devices, officers or collision avoidance. Think of a ladder that tightens with each step. When you see one of these signs, ask what you are stopping for and whether you will stay aboard. Next we cover places where you may never park.

why_how.text: Some places are off limits for parking, stopping and standing alike.
Other places ban parking and standing, each with its own distance.

scenario.text: Jamal sees an open spot right beside a fire hydrant and plans to leave the car empty.

reasoning.text: Nothing may park, stop or stand within fifteen feet of a hydrant unless a licensed driver stays aboard, and no licensed driver will stay aboard.

result.text: He moves on and finds a spot farther away.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the same short distance applies to every hazard.

correction.text: Hydrants clear fifteen feet, crosswalks and firehouse drives twenty, lights and signs thirty, and rail crossings fifty.

memory_support.text: Fifteen hydrant, twenty crosswalk, thirty sign, fifty rail.

prompt.text: How close to a stop sign may you park or stand?

rationale.text: Lights and stop or yield signs clear thirty feet, one of the four key distances.

lines.text: Where nothing may park, stop or stand.
Where parking and standing are banned.

narration.text: This lesson covers the places where the manual says you may not leave your car. There are two lists. The first is stricter: places where nothing may park, stop or stand at all. The second covers places where parking and standing are banned, and it comes with several distances to remember. Those distances are easy to confuse, so we will finish by lining up four of them side by side: hydrants, crosswalks and firehouse drives, lights and signs, and railroad crossings. Knowing illegal parking is part of what the road test expects, so these lists are worth learning well.

lines.text: Within fifteen feet of a hydrant.
In intersections, on rails, bridges, tunnels.

narration.text: Start with the strictest list. Nothing may park, stop or stand within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant, unless a licensed driver stays aboard. The same ban covers double parking, sidewalks and crosswalks, and intersections unless you have permission. It also covers railroad tracks, spots beside road work where you would block traffic, anywhere within thirty feet of a safety zone, and bridges and tunnels. In all of these places the rule is the same: do not leave the car there, and do not even halt there briefly, except in the hydrant case with a licensed driver still in the car.

lines.text: Before driveways and along cut curbs.
Twenty feet of crosswalks, firehouse drives.
Thirty of signals; no parking fifty rail.

narration.text: The second list bans parking and standing. You may not park or stand in front of a driveway or along a cut curb. Stay at least twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, and thirty feet from traffic lights and stop or yield signs. Near a firehouse, stay twenty feet from its driveway on the same side, and seventy-five feet away when you are across the street from it. Separately, parking is prohibited within fifty feet of a railroad crossing. Notice that the earlier list covers parking and standing, so it is a different list from the strict one, where even stopping is banned.

lines.text: Lights and signs: thirty. Rail: fifty.

narration.text: Here is the trap: these numbers blur together. The manual pairs four distances with four hazards so you can keep them straight. Hydrants clear fifteen feet. Intersection crosswalks and firehouse driveways clear twenty feet. Traffic lights and stop or yield signs clear thirty feet. Railroad crossings clear fifty feet. A useful way to hold them is that the numbers rise as you go from hydrant to crosswalk to sign to rail. Remember too that seventy-five feet is a separate case, for parking across the street from a firehouse driveway. Do not let that number replace one of the four.

lines.text: Hydrant ban eases with a driver aboard.
Do not block traffic beside work.

narration.text: Two details from the strict list deserve a second look. The hydrant rule has one exception: the fifteen-foot ban on parking, stopping and standing applies unless a licensed driver stays aboard. So you may not leave a car by a hydrant, but a car with a licensed driver in it is treated differently. The same strict list also keeps you thirty feet from a safety zone, which is a different place from the signals and signs on the other list, even though the distance is the same. And beside road work, the ban applies where your car would block traffic.

lines.text: You want to park near a stop sign.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you find a space on a street just before a stop sign. How close to the sign may you park or stand? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no closer than thirty feet. The manual bans parking and standing within thirty feet of traffic lights and stop or yield signs. If you said fifteen feet, that is the hydrant distance. Twenty feet belongs to crosswalks at intersections and firehouse driveways, and fifty feet belongs to railroad crossings. Matching each hazard to its own distance is the key to this whole lesson.

lines.text: Strict list: no park, stop or stand.
Second list: no park or stand.

narration.text: To wrap up, the strictest list bans parking, stopping and standing within fifteen feet of a hydrant unless a licensed driver stays aboard, double-parked, on sidewalks and crosswalks, in intersections without permission, on rails, where you block traffic beside work, within thirty feet of safety zones, and on bridges and in tunnels. The second list bans parking and standing before driveways, along cut curbs, and at set distances. Hydrants fifteen, crosswalks and firehouse drives twenty, lights and signs thirty, rail crossings fifty, with seventy-five across from a firehouse drive. Next we cover disability parking.

why_how.text: Disability spaces are reserved for the named holder of a plate or permit who is aboard the vehicle.
Lying to get plates or permits carries real penalties, on two different tracks.

scenario.text: Dev's grandmother has a disability permit, and Dev borrows her car to run an errand alone.

reasoning.text: The space needs a plate or permit with the named holder aboard an operating vehicle, and she is not with him.

result.text: Dev parks in a regular space instead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the permit or plate alone lets anyone driving the car use the space.

correction.text: The named holder must be aboard an operating vehicle, on streets and in larger shopping centers alike.

memory_support.text: Plate lies cost the license; permit lies cost money.

prompt.text: What happens to someone who lies to get disability plates?

answer.text: It is a misdemeanor with mandatory revocation, plus a fine, jail or both and a surcharge.

rationale.text: Plate lies follow the criminal track that costs the license, while permit lies bring civil penalties.

narration.text: This lesson covers parking spaces reserved for people with disabilities. The manual sets out who may use them, how plates and permits are requested, how the spaces and the striped aisles beside them are marked, and what happens to people who lie to get plates or permits. It also gives the default fines for parking violations in shopping centers. We will finish with a quick look at the topics the chapter's own review questions cover. The details matter, especially the rule about who must be in the car, so we will start there and then work through the forms, the aisles, the penalties and the fines.

lines.text: DMV plates, a local permit, or equivalent.
The named holder must be aboard.

narration.text: A disability space demands one of three things: DMV plates, a local permit, or an equivalent from another state. That alone is not enough. The named holder must be aboard an operating vehicle. So if the person the plate or permit belongs to is not in the car, the space is not yours to use, even if the plate or permit is on the car. The manual applies this rule on streets and in larger shopping centers alike, so it does not change when you pull into a big store's lot. Keep the picture simple: right credential, and its holder aboard.

lines.text: Form MV six six four point one.
Reserved spaces wear signs, maybe paint.

narration.text: To ask for disability plates or a permit, the manual names one form, written in the manual as MV six six four point one. Reserved spaces are marked with signs and may also be painted. Beside many of them you will see an access aisle with diagonal stripes. That aisle must stay empty, because it gives room for wheelchairs and special equipment to get in and out of a vehicle. It is not extra parking. Signs, possible paint and the striped aisle together mark the reserved area, and the aisle part of it is kept clear for access.

The manual treats lying to get plates or permits seriously. Lying for disability plates is a misdemeanor. It brings mandatory license revocation, plus a fine, jail or both, and a surcharge. Lying for a permit draws civil penalties of two hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, plus a surcharge. Both penalties reach the applicant and the certifying doctor alike, so the person who signs off on a false claim is exposed too. In short, plate fraud is handled as a crime that costs the license, while permit fraud is handled with money penalties. That split is the point of the next slide.

Here is the trap. Because plates and permits do the same job, people assume lying for either one is punished the same way. The manual describes two different tracks. Plates need the holder aboard, and lying for them costs the license through a misdemeanor with mandatory revocation. Permit lies cost money, through civil penalties plus a surcharge. So the criminal track goes with plates, and the civil track goes with permits. If a question asks which lie leads to license revocation, the answer is the lie for plates. If it asks about the dollar range, that is the permit.

Who sets the fine for a parking violation? On the street, municipalities price the violations. In shopping centers there is a default: fifty to seventy-five dollars for a first offense, and seventy-five to one hundred fifty dollars for a second offense within two years in one town, each plus a thirty-dollar surcharge. The chapter then closes with review questions on curb distance, road-side doors, preparing to leave a space, what no stopping means, passenger loading under the no-series signs, and mid-block crosswalks. Those topics map neatly onto the lessons you have just worked through.

lines.text: Someone lied to get disability plates.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver lied on an application to get disability plates. What can happen to them? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that it is a misdemeanor with mandatory license revocation, plus a fine, jail or both, and a surcharge. That is the criminal track, and it goes with plates. If you answered a civil penalty of two hundred fifty to one thousand dollars, that is the penalty for lying to get a permit, which costs money rather than the license. Remember too that the certifying doctor faces these penalties alongside the applicant.

To close, a disability space needs DMV plates, a local permit or an out-of-state equivalent, with the named holder aboard an operating vehicle, on streets and in larger shopping centers alike. Plates and permits are sought on form MV six six four point one, spaces wear signs and maybe paint, and striped access aisles stay empty. Lying for plates is a misdemeanor with mandatory revocation, while lying for a permit brings civil penalties, against applicant and doctor alike. Towns price street violations, and shopping centers have a default fine ladder plus a surcharge. That completes this chapter.
